tools.name: pmf_scorecard
tools.description: Helps you decide whether you have product market fit and whether to scale: it takes your product, target market and current metrics (MRR, ACV, churn, NPS, CAC, LTV, retention, activation and similar) and returns a scorecard that scores each dimension against example benchmark ranges. It also gives priority actions and the data gaps to fill, reads the business model from your inputs, leaves the activation score out for services, connectivity and investment businesses, and quotes and answers your customer feedback.

target_market.description: Benchmark segment for scoring (for example enterprise SaaS, telecom or logistics tech). Ask the user to confirm it when it differs from the product description. The selected benchmark and its stated fallback ranges are used; the output explains conflicts. The separate sector choice controls sector notes.

current_metrics.description: Your current metrics, written as text (the tool reads the figures from it). Include any of: MRR, ARR, ACV, churn rate, NPS, CAC, LTV, retention rate, activation rate, DAU/MAU, trial conversion, revenue growth. Example: 'MRR: $50K, Churn: 3%, NPS: 45, CAC: $500, LTV: $3000, Retention: 92%'. A figure that no rule scores is listed as not scored

time_in_market.description: How long the product has been in market (shown in the scorecard)

customer_feedback.description: Optional: Qualitative feedback themes, one per line or separated by semicolons (for example 'Customers like X; they struggle with Y'). Each theme is quoted and answered

business_model.description: Optional: how you earn revenue, so the advice fits it (saas, services, connectivity, transactions, marketplace, hardware_software or investment). Leave it out and the tool reads it from your other inputs and says how it read it

your_sector.description: Optional: your company's own industry (not your customers'). When given, it decides the sector notes; when left out, the tool reads it from your words and stays neutral if they are unclear.

tools.title: PMF Scorecard

tools.name: launch_commander
tools.description: Helps you decide your launch plan: it takes what you are launching, the launch type, your target segments and your goals, and returns a phased launch plan with tasks, a messaging table and success metrics. Give a date for a dated timeline, or 'TBD' or a quarter such as 'Q2 2027' for a flexible plan. Tasks and messaging follow the sector and business model read from your inputs, and each goal is filed under its own metric.

product_feature.description: What you're launching (product/feature name and description)

launch_date.description: Target launch date. Accepts: 'YYYY-MM-DD', 'Q1 2027', 'March 2027', or 'TBD' for planning mode

launch_type.description: Type of launch determines plan complexity

goals.description: Launch success metrics (for example '40 qualified meetings, $300K pipeline, 5 reference customers')

available_channels.description: Optional: Marketing channels available (comma-separated). E.g., 'email, linkedin, blog, webinar, PR, paid_ads, community'

team_size.description: Marketing/GTM team size affects task distribution

business_model.description: Optional: how you earn revenue, so the advice fits it (saas, services, connectivity, transactions, marketplace, hardware_software or investment). Leave it out and the tool reads it from your other inputs and says how it read it

industry.description: Optional: your own company's sector, so the answer uses the usual buyers, measures and objections for what you sell. Leave it out and the tool reads the sector from your other inputs and names what it read

your_sector.description: Optional: your company's own industry (not your customers'). When given, it decides the sector notes; when left out, the tool reads it from your words and stays neutral if they are unclear.

tools.title: Launch Commander

tools.name: customer_interview_kit
tools.description: Helps you decide what to ask customers to test your hunch: it takes the interview type, the product context and the person you are interviewing, and returns an interview guide that fits the interview type, the sector and the product complexity. Questions use the sector's own language (the sector is chosen, or read from your inputs), your hypotheses are kept whole, and synthesis templates are included.

interview_type.description: Type of interview determines question focus

industry.description: Industry affects terminology and context. Leave it out and the sector is read from your other inputs

key_hypotheses.description: Optional: Hypotheses to validate during interview, one per line or separated by semicolons

business_model.description: Optional: how you earn revenue, so the advice fits it (saas, services, connectivity, transactions, marketplace, hardware_software or investment). Leave it out and the tool reads it from your other inputs and says how it read it

your_sector.description: Optional: your company's own industry (not your customers'). When given, it decides the sector notes; when left out, the tool reads it from your words and stays neutral if they are unclear.

tools.title: Customer Interview Kit

tools.name: retention_playbook
tools.description: Helps you decide why customers leave and what to do about each reason: it takes your customer segment, business model and current churn rate, and returns a retention playbook with health signals, interventions and an email draft for each churn reason. If you do not know why customers leave, leave the churn reasons out and you get a churn discovery kit instead. Your current interventions and data signals are used when you give them.

business_model.description: Business model affects health score weighting. enterprise_contract is read further from your text when it names services, connectivity or investment

churn_reasons.description: Optional: known churn reasons, comma-separated. If you do not know them, leave this blank and you get a churn discovery kit with a framework for finding the reasons

available_data_signals.description: What you can track (comma-separated). E.g., 'login frequency, support tickets, SLA attainment, QBR attendance'

cs_team_size.description: CS team capacity affects intervention strategy

current_interventions.description: Optional: What retention tactics you already do (listed and compared with the playbook)

product.description: Optional: Your product or company name, used in the title and the email drafts

industry.description: Optional: your own company's sector, so the answer uses the usual buyers, measures and objections for what you sell. Leave it out and the tool reads the sector from your other inputs and names what it read

your_sector.description: Optional: your company's own industry (not your customers'). When given, it decides the sector notes; when left out, the tool reads it from your words and stays neutral if they are unclear.

tools.title: Retention Playbook

tools.name: partner_architect
tools.description: Helps you decide what partner program to run and how to start it: it takes your company, product, partner model, partner goal and deal size, and returns a partner program with tiers, example commission amounts and KPIs. The structure differs for resellers, referrals, integrations, agencies, affiliates and white label, uses your existing partners when given, and names the partner types that fit your sector's buying committee.

partner_goals.description: Revenue/growth targets from partners (shown as the target of the first KPI row)

your_deal_size.description: Average deal size as one amount (e.g., '$5000 ACV', '$5K' or '$500/month'; a range is refused). It scales the example commission amounts; the example rates are fixed

partner_support_capacity.description: How much partner support can you provide?

existing_partners.description: Optional: Current partner types/count, one per line or separated by semicolons (listed in the plan)

business_model.description: Optional: how you earn revenue, so the advice fits it (saas, services, connectivity, transactions, marketplace, hardware_software or investment). Leave it out and the tool reads it from your other inputs and says how it read it

industry.description: Optional: your own company's sector, so the answer uses the usual buyers, measures and objections for what you sell. Leave it out and the tool reads the sector from your other inputs and names what it read

your_sector.description: Optional: your company's own industry (not your customers'). When given, it decides the sector notes; when left out, the tool reads it from your words and stays neutral if they are unclear.

tools.title: Partner Architect

tools.name: crisis_planner
tools.description: Helps you decide who does what when a crisis hits: it takes your company, industry, customer base and data sensitivity, and returns crisis playbooks with a response team and notification steps for each crisis. Name the crises you know of to get those playbooks; without them it uses a default set of common crises for your sector, not ranked by likelihood. Each compliance item you list is used in the notification steps.

industry.description: Industry affects which crises to prioritize

potential_crises.description: Optional: crisis types to plan for, comma-separated. If not provided, the tool uses a default set of common crises for your sector (not ranked by likelihood). Options: data_breach, service_outage, sla_breach, regulatory_action, fraud_incident, ai_wrong_action, pr_incident, executive_departure, security_vulnerability, customer_data_exposure, product_safety

compliance_requirements.description: Optional: Relevant compliance, comma-separated (for example ISO 27001, SOC 2, GDPR). Each item is named in the notification steps

business_model.description: Optional: how you earn revenue, so the advice fits it (saas, services, connectivity, transactions, marketplace, hardware_software or investment). Leave it out and the tool reads it from your other inputs and says how it read it

your_sector.description: Optional: your company's own industry (not your customers'). When given, it decides the sector notes; when left out, the tool reads it from your words and stays neutral if they are unclear.

tools.title: Crisis Planner

tools.name: competitive_intel
tools.description: Helps you decide how to win against each competitor: it takes your product and the competitors you name, and returns one battle card per competitor built from your strengths, weaknesses, competitor details, objections, wins and losses. Each competitor detail goes to the competitor it names, each objection gets its own answer, and strengths and gaps taken from wins and losses stay in your own words.

your_product.description: Your product name and brief description

competitors.description: Competitor names, comma-separated. You get one battle card for each competitor named

your_strengths.description: Optional: what you do better, comma-separated. Taken from your wins, in your own words, if not provided

your_weaknesses.description: Optional: where competitors beat you, comma-separated. Taken from your losses, in your own words, if not provided

competitor_details.description: Optional: Any known details about competitors, one per line or separated by semicolons. E.g., 'Competitor A is cheaper; Competitor B targets enterprise'. Each detail goes to the competitor it names

common_objections.description: Sales objections you hear (comma-separated). E.g., 'too expensive, missing X feature, competitor has better Y'

recent_wins.description: Why customers chose you over competitors: used as your strengths when none are given

recent_losses.description: Why you lost deals to competitors: used as your gaps when none are given

business_model.description: Optional: how you earn revenue, so the advice fits it (saas, services, connectivity, transactions, marketplace, hardware_software or investment). Leave it out and the tool reads it from your other inputs and says how it read it

industry.description: Optional: your own company's sector, so the answer uses the usual buyers, measures and objections for what you sell. Leave it out and the tool reads the sector from your other inputs and names what it read

your_sector.description: Optional: your company's own industry (not your customers'). When given, it decides the sector notes; when left out, the tool reads it from your words and stays neutral if they are unclear.

tools.title: Competitive Intel

tools.name: craft_gtm_analyzer
tools.description: Helps you decide whether a GTM plan is clear enough to run: it takes the text of a GTM document or plan and returns a score for each CRAFT dimension, based only on what the plan contains. Timeline counts real dates, durations and quarters; the answer shows the plan's own line for each dimension, names only the elements that are missing and suggests sections to add.

document_content.description: The GTM document or plan to analyze. Paste the full text: the tool reads it and scores it against the framework

document_type.description: Type of document (shown in the analysis)

intended_audience.description: Optional: Who will read/approve this document

desired_outcome.description: Optional: What action should this document drive

industry.description: Optional: your own company's sector, so the answer uses the usual buyers, measures and objections for what you sell. Leave it out and the tool reads the sector from your other inputs and names what it read

your_sector.description: Optional: your company's own industry (not your customers'). When given, it decides the sector notes; when left out, the tool reads it from your words and stays neutral if they are unclear.

tools.title: CRAFT GTM Analyzer

tools.name: scale_paid_check
tools.description: Helps you decide whether to scale paid now: it takes your customer list (signing date, segment, monthly fee and any stop or return dates) and your churn reasons, and returns, for each customer group, scale, run a capped test, or hold, with the counts behind it, the stop rule, payback, a first draft response to each churn reason and a churn interview guide.

business_model.description: Business model, passed on to retention_playbook

as_of.description: The date the list was pulled (YYYY-MM-DD)

customers.description: One row per customer (1 to 2000 items)

monthly_fee.description: Monthly fee at signing (annual contracts: the yearly fee divided by 12)

stopped.description: Optional: the first date a payment was due and not paid (for annual contracts, the renewal date they did not renew), YYYY-MM-DD

resumed.description: Optional: date they paid again, if they came back (YYYY-MM-DD)

monthly_starts.description: Optional: activity in each of the 12 months before as_of (or before stopped), for the seasonal tag

metrics.description: Optional: each metric with its name, value, whether it counts customers or revenue, and its period

counts.description: Optional: whether the metric counts customers or revenue

period.description: Optional: period over which the metric is measured

stop_line.description: Optional (default 0.80): share of a cohort that must still pay at month 12. 0.80 is Shashwat's example line for a $36,000 contract, not a benchmark.

payback_line_months.description: Optional (default 12): the longest acceptable paid payback in months. 12 is Shashwat's example line for a $36,000 contract, not a benchmark.

gross_margin.description: Optional (0 to 1): gross margin needed for the money section

blended_cac.description: Optional: blended CAC, shown for contrast only

test_cap.description: Optional: all-in budget for a capped test

win_rate_floor.description: Optional (0 to 1): a win rate the buyer is confident paid can reach

win_rate_target.description: Optional (0 to 1): the highest win rate the buyer would believe

churn_reasons.description: Reasons in customers' words, comma or line separated

interview_persona.description: Role to interview, for the interview kit

tools.title: Scale Paid Check

tools.name: segment_and_seat_cut_check
tools.description: Helps you decide which customer segment to back, and whether your pricing is safe if AI cuts seats: it takes each segment's ACV, sales cycle, accounts, deal source and CAC, its logo, gross and net retention, how you charge in your own words, and your seller ramp, cost and qualified demand, and returns one page per segment with payback, gross profit per dollar of CAC, seller capacity after ramp and cycle, and the renewal if customers cut a share of seats. Ask the person to confirm the segment split, their own win rate and what customers can cut before marking each as confirmed; anything not confirmed or not given is shown as missing, never guessed.

product.description: What you sell, in one line

gross_margin_percent.description: Gross margin as a percent (for example 72). Needed for payback and every profit sum

tracks_expansion.description: Optional: true only if the company tracks expansion account by account. It adds a later years table below the pages. Payback on CAC and ARR always leads

business_stage.description: Optional: funding stage, passed to the motion first draft (for example series-a)

industry.description: Optional: your industry, passed to the motion first draft

segments.description: One item per customer segment (1 to 4). Split by who signs, how they find you, sales cycle and contract value

name.description: The segment in your own words (for example 'banks and insurers with 200 to 2,000 contact centre agents')

acv.description: Average contract value per year, in dollars

sales_cycle_days.description: Days from first meeting to signature

accounts.description: Number of accounts that could buy in this segment

deal_source.description: Where most deals in this segment come from (for example inbound, outbound, referrals, partnerships or mixed)

cac.description: Cost to win one customer in this segment, in dollars

logo_retention_percent.description: Share of customers still paying after a year, as a percent (for example 89)

gross_retention_percent.description: Gross revenue retention as a percent: opening revenue less churn and downgrades, over opening revenue (for example 92). It cannot pass 100

net_retention_percent.description: Net revenue retention as a percent: gross retention plus expansion (for example 108)

monthly_logo_churn_percent.description: Optional: share of customers lost in a month, as a percent (for example 2.5). Used for the simple lifetime sum; left out, yearly logo retention is used

pricing_unit_in_writing.description: What you bill on, in your own words (for example 'per agent seat, billed yearly' or 'per resolved contact')

pricing_unit.description: Optional: the pricing unit, if you want to state it directly. It overrides the reading of your sentence

seat_share_of_acv_percent.description: Optional, for a mix of seats and usage: the percent of the contract billed on seats (for example 60)

what_customers_can_cut.description: What a customer can cut, and when, in your own words (for example 'seats, at each yearly renewal')

icp_match_percent.description: Optional: percent of accounts that match your ideal customer profile, passed to the sizing first draft

year_one_share_percent.description: Optional: the year one share you assume, as a percent, passed to the sizing first draft

win_rate_percent.description: Your own win rate: the percent of qualified opportunities you win in this segment, from your closed deals (for example 33). Used only when the person has confirmed it

year_one_customer_target.description: Optional: new customers you want from this segment in year one. Left out, the customer count from the sizing first draft is used

seller_ramp_months.description: Months before a new seller carries a full pipeline

seller_loaded_cost_per_year.description: Full yearly cost of one seller, in dollars

ramped_deals_per_seller_per_year.description: Deals a fully ramped seller closes in a year in this segment, from your own record

monthly_qualified_demand.description: Qualified opportunities assigned to sellers each month in this segment

seat_cut_percent.description: Optional: the percent of seats a customer could cut if AI does more of the work (for example 25). Used only when the person has confirmed it

arr_share_cutting_percent.description: Optional: the percent of this segment's revenue held by accounts that would make that cut (for example 32)

seats_per_account.description: Optional: seats in an average account

work_units_per_seat_per_year.description: Optional: units of work one seat handles in a year (for example contacts, shipments or claims)

buyer_cost_per_seat_per_year.description: Optional: what one seat costs the buyer in a year, in salary and overhead, in dollars

usage_price_per_unit.description: Optional: a price per unit of work you want to test, in dollars

run_cost_per_unit.description: Optional: your cost to run one unit of work, in dollars

gross_retention_gate_percent.description: Optional: your own gross retention line for releasing more money (for example 90)

net_retention_gate_percent.description: Optional: your own net retention line (for example 100)

logo_retention_gate_percent.description: Optional: your own logo retention line (for example 85)

churn_reasons.description: Optional: why customers in this segment leave or shrink, in their words, separated by semicolons

motion_lead.description: Optional: the lead motion from the EPIC audit on GTM Alpha, as it came back

motion_score.description: Optional: the score of that lead motion, 1 to 10

motion_reason.description: Optional: the audit's reason line for the lead motion, as it came back

sizing_tam.description: Optional: TAM in dollars from the sizing calculator on ICP Intelligence

sizing_sam.description: Optional: SAM in dollars from the sizing calculator

sizing_som.description: Optional: year one SOM in dollars from the sizing calculator

sizing_year_one_customers.description: Optional: customers needed in year one, from the sizing calculator

confirmed.description: What the person has confirmed. Set each to true only after asking them. Until the segment split is confirmed no sum runs

segment_split.description: The person confirmed the segments are how their closed deals really divide

win_rate.description: The person confirmed the win rates are their own, from closed deals

seat_cut.description: The person confirmed what customers can cut, and the share of seats to test

tools.title: Segment and Seat Cut Check
